text: Ralph Edward Flanders (September 28, 1880 – February 19, 1970) was an American mechanical engineer, industrialist, and Republican U.S. Senator from Vermont. Born in Barnet, Vermont, on September 28, 1880, he was the oldest of nine children of Albert W. Flanders and Mary (Gilfillan) Flanders. When he was six, his family moved to Lincoln, Rhode Island, where his father farmed and managed the manufacture and sales of a bookrack he designed. Flanders attended school in Providence and Central Falls and graduated from Central Falls High School in 1896. Unable to afford college, his father arranged a two-year apprenticeship at the Brown & Sharpe Manufacturing Company, where he learned machining and drafting, supplemented by courses at the International Correspondence Schools and the Rhode Island School of Design. He later worked for various machine tool companies in New England and served as a draftsman for General Electric in Lynn, Massachusetts until 1905, when he moved to New York City to become editor of Machine magazine, a role he held from 1905 to 1910. During this time, he wrote extensively on topics such as gear tooth systems, gear cutting machinery, hobs, can manufacturing, and automobile production, including Machine's reference series. In 1909, while working on a definitive book about gear cutting machinery, he suffered a "nervous breakdown" and took time off; in 1910, he moved to Springfield, Vermont, to work as a mechanical engineer for the Fellows Gear Shaper Company. There, he became friendly with James Hartness, president of the Jones & Lamson Machine Company (J&L), and married Hartness' daughter, Helen in 1911. Hartness later hired Flanders as manager of the department that built the Fay automatic lathe, which Flanders redesigned for higher productivity and accuracy. He became a director in 1912 and president of J&L in 1933 after Hartness retired. As president, he implemented a continuous production line for the Hartness Turret Lathe and acquired and assigned over twenty patents to the company. Flanders and his brother Ernest developed screw thread grinding machines, incorporating advances in thread technology and engineering calculations, which earned them the Edward Longstreth Medal of the Franklin Institute in 1942. This work improved the manufacture of die-cut screws in soft metal and solved thread-grinding on hardened work, and also enabled rapid production of turbine blades, aiding General Electric in manufacturing jet engines. Flanders became president of the National Machine-Tool Builders Association in 1923, served as president of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) from 1934 to 1936, was vice president of the American Engineering Council in 1937, and chaired the Screw-Thread Committee of the American Standards Association throughout the 1930s. In 1944, ASME awarded him the Hoover Medal for public service in social, civic, and humanitarian efforts, and the British Institution of Mechanical Engineers made him an honorary member. In 1917, he served in the Machine-Tool Section of the War Industries Board. During the Great Depression, he began writing on social policy, focusing on human development in a technological era and advocating for a "program of human values" to achieve a good life, while maintaining a goal of "full employment" grounded in economic principles. In 1933, he was appointed to the Business Advisory Council by Secretary of Commerce Daniel Roper, becoming chairman of the Committee on Unemployment, which recommended addressing unemployment geographically and by industry; however, President Roosevelt prioritized Supreme Court expansion and chose the undistributed profits tax instead, a decision Flanders viewed as discouraging capital investment. He was also appointed to the industrial advisory board of the National Recovery Administration (NRA) in 1933, where he opposed a proposal to cut worker hours by 10% and raise wages by 10% to spread employment, a policy that ultimately did not prevail. In 1937, Governor George Aiken appointed him to the Special Milk Investigative Committee and as chairman of the Flood Control Commission, which negotiated with other New England states to share costs for flood-control dams following the 1927 floods. In 1940, he was elected president of the New England Council, which studied industry and commerce in the region, and he used this role to raise awareness of the potential for U.S. involvement in the Second World War. In 1942, he joined the Committee for Economic Development (CED), helping shape its recommendations to Congress on the roles of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund. From the 1930s onward, he held board positions with the Shawmut Bank (1938–41), Federal Reserve Bank of Boston (1941–44), Boston and Maine Railroad, National Life Insurance Company, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and Norwich University. In 1944, he was elected president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, during which time the bank helped establish the Boston Port Authority to revitalize New England's cargo shipping capacity. In 1946, with Georges Doriot, Karl Compton, and others, he co-founded American Research & Development (AR&D), the first venture capital company to invest in a pool of fledgling companies according to defined rules and goals; Flanders served as a director. In 1940, Flanders ran an unsuccessful campaign for the U.S. Senate against George Aiken, the popular two-term Vermont governor. Although he admired Aiken, he believed Aiken's "liberal" views would not aid economic recovery. The campaign was described as dirty and mean by The Rutland Herald, with accusations that Flanders sold arms to the Nazis and claims that Aiken was influenced by his assistant. Flanders later reflected that he had allowed his campaign advisers to make too many decisions, including a brochure showing him wearing a three-piece suit with a piglet, which appeared phony to Vermonters given the state's subsistence farming culture. Aiken won by 7,000 votes, spending $3,219.50 compared to Flanders's $18,698.45. In August 1946, incumbent Senator Warren Austin resigned to become U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations, and Flanders won the August 13 Republican primary, which was effectively the election in Vermont. Governor Mortimer R. Proctor appointed Flanders to complete the remainder of Austin's term, giving him seniority over freshman senators elected on the same day. Flanders easily won the November 5 election, receiving 75% of the vote to Charles P. McDevitt's 25%, and was overwhelmingly reelected in 1952 with 72% to Allan R. Johnston's 28%. He declined to seek a third term in 1958. Flanders' voting record was more conservative than that of his colleague George Aiken and reflected his business background. In his second term, a Republican majority allowed him to serve on the Joint Economic Committee, the Finance Committee, and the Committee on Armed Services. Though a conservative, he supported constructive competition between conservatism and liberalism, viewing liberalism as focused on individual welfare and freedom, while conservatism preserved collective institutions. He believed conservatives could offer "reasoned objections" to emotionally driven liberal proposals. He had a Congregationalist religious upbringing that evolved into a belief in "moral law," which he considered as essential to social achievement as physical law. He defined moral law as requiring honesty, compassion, responsibility, cooperation, humility, and wisdom—values shared across cultures—and spoke of a "Presence" or "daimon" that guided his actions. He viewed the Marshall Plan as an application of moral law, arguing its true purpose was to counter Communism through economic restoration in Europe, not to provide relief, enhance gratitude, or boost U.S. prestige. In 1945, during testimony on the Employment Act (of 1946), he defined the "right to a job" as a shared responsibility among individuals, labor, businesses, and governments, and recommended that wage increases be tied to productivity gains, with gains split three ways—wages, profits, and lower prices—to benefit all parties. He believed this approach required mutual respect and understanding between labor and management. Flanders maintained amicable relations with organized labor and welcomed the United Electrical Workers Union into Jones & Lamson Machine Company, making it the first unionized company in Springfield, Vermont. He met with President Roosevelt on several occasions and criticized his failure to heed warnings about a surprise attack on Pearl Harbor and his underestimation of the Communist threat in China, particularly at the 1943 Tehran Conference. He acknowledged Roosevelt's political genius but opposed his advocacy of raising taxes and believed large social programs were ineffective. In his autobiography, he explored opportunities for government funding of public housing and higher education and voted in favor of the Civil Rights Act of 1957. National Cold War policy deeply interested him; he was concerned about the global spread of Communism without military conflict. He viewed President Truman as generally competent but hampered by the Roosevelt legacy of appeasement toward the Soviets and criticized his attempt to unite Nationalist and Communist Chinese factions. He supported the Marshall Plan to prevent Communist influence in Western Europe but criticized Secretary of State John Foster Dulles for failing to build friendly alliances with Egypt and India, which instead aligned with the Soviet Union. He believed spending 62% of federal income on defense was irrational given the Soviet claim to avoid nuclear conflict and advocated for the development of "atomic- and hydrogen" technologies.

Flanders believed that government, not private, action should address national issues and considered large social programs ineffective. In his autobiography, he described exploring government funding for public housing and higher education. He voted in favor of the Civil Rights Act of 1957. National Cold War policy deeply interested him; he was concerned about the global spread of Communism without military force and believed President Truman was generally good but limited by Roosevelt’s policy of appeasing the Soviets. He viewed Truman’s effort to unite Nationalist and Communist Chinese factions as mistaken and supported the Marshall Plan to prevent Communist influence in Western Europe. However, he criticized Secretary of State John Foster Dulles for failing to build friendly ties with Egypt and India, which instead aligned with the Soviet Union. Flanders argued that spending 62% of federal income on defense was irrational given the Soviet claim to avoid nuclear conflict, advocating instead that atomic and hydrogen bomb development be matched with equally intense disarmament negotiations, with cooperation from the Soviet government on armament control being paramount. He was an early and strong critic of Senator Joseph McCarthy, condemning his misdirection in the fight against communism and his damage to U.S. international respect. Flanders believed the nation should focus outward on the global advance of Communist power, which he saw as threatening the United States and Canada as the last free world remnants. On March 9, 1954, he delivered a speech on the Senate floor expressing these views, which was widely praised and caused a flood of support, with messages calling it a display of Vermont courage, humor, and decency and one that brought "a breath of fresh clean air from the Green Mountains." Senators John Sherman Cooper and Herbert Lehman commended him, and a national publication noted the Republican Party’s presence of courageous moral leadership. However, some reactions were negative, with critics suggesting retribution for McCarthy’s opponents and calling McCarthy a "demigod above the law," stating that disagreement equated to being "RED." William Loeb of the Burlington Daily News criticized Flanders as "stupid" for supporting Democratic positions on McCarthy. On June 1, 1954, Flanders addressed the Senate criticizing McCarthy as "Dennis the Menace," accusing him of dividing the nation and drawing parallels between communist victories in Asia and the U.S. being subjected to internal division and spying. He claimed McCarthy’s actions were a "colossal innocence" and a sign of communist strategy. On June 11, 1954, Flanders introduced a resolution charging McCarthy with unbecoming conduct and calling for his removal from committee, later modifying it to align with prior censure actions. The resolution condemned McCarthy for obstructing Senate constitutional processes and acting contrary to senatorial ethics by slandering a committee and its chairman. A group of 23 top businessmen, labor leaders, and educators urged all senators (except McCarthy) to support the censure. The Senate censured McCarthy on December 2, 1954 by a vote of 65 to 22, with Senate Republicans split 22 to 22. A 1990 Rutland Herald article noted that Vermont’s reaction to Flanders’s role in the censure was "sour," concluding that his convictions did not match the priorities of his constituents, who saw the issue as "not our problem." In 1911, Flanders married Helen Edith Hartness, daughter of inventor James Hartness, and they lived in Springfield, Vermont, when he became president of Jones & Lamson. They had three children: Elizabeth (born 1912), Anna (Nancy, born 1918), and James (born 1923). Flanders authored or coauthored eight books, including his autobiography, *Senator from Vermont*, covering topics such as unemployment, inflation, labor-management cooperation, and the belief that "moral law is natural law" and should be part of education. His papers are held at the Special Collections Research Center at Syracuse University Library and the Special Collections of the University of Vermont’s Bailey-Howe Library. He received over sixteen honorary degrees from institutions including Stevens Institute of Technology (M.E.), Dartmouth College (M.S., LL.D.), Harvard University (LL.D.), Middlebury College (D.Sc.), and the University of Vermont (D.Eng.). His wife, Helen Hartness Flanders, was a folk song collector and author of books on New England ballads. Flanders died in Springfield on February 19, 1970 and was buried at Summer Hill Cemetery in Springfield alongside his wife and members of the Hartness family. His Senate legacy continues to influence Vermont politicians; in 2001, Senator Jim Jeffords cited Flanders three times, calling him one of five Vermont politicians who spoke their minds and guided the party toward fundamental principles. In speeches to Georgetown University Law Center and Johnson State College, Senator Patrick Leahy cited Flanders as one of three Vermont politicians who demonstrated standing firm in beliefs, that conflict need not be adversarial, and who rose against abuses of American rights when unpopular. In 2016, Vermont Congressman Peter Welch cited Flanders as a model for resisting policies of the Donald Trump Administration, stating he stood up and said "no, this has got to end."
